content:
The night the Limmat gave up a body, the rain came down soft and mean, the way it does over the Old Town when it has no intention of stopping.

It was late — past midnight, I think, though in the city hall corridor the clock had already become meaningless. Someone from the river police had rung the station: something floating near the Seefeld, caught by the bend where the current slows before the water narrows. I was still buttoning my coat when they told me it was a man.

By the time I got to the bank, the lamps from the patrol boat were slicing through the mist, and the river looked less like water than like black oil being stirred by something patient. The men had already brought the body onto the towpath. It was curled on its side, the water still running out of the coat in little, obscene streams. The face was upturned. A young man, maybe thirty, with a good suit and ruined shoes. His fingers were stiff, but not so cold that I could not feel the last of the night in them.

I knelt beside him, and for a moment I only listened: the rain, the distant moan of a barge, the weak coughing of a police officer standing under his cap. The smell was river, sewage, and something underneath that I did not like. There was a mark on his throat, narrow and clean, and blood had gone down into the water and come back in the folds of his collar like a dark lace.

“Who is he?” I asked.

The river police officer shook his head. “No papers. Nothing in the pockets. Maybe a watch.”

They had already taken it out, I saw. A good watch. Silver case, slightly dented. The kind a man wears because he wants to be recognized by it.

I stood and looked along the bank. The city was still awake in patches: a tram sliding past with its red numbers glowing in the fog, a bar near the bridge letting out smoke and laughter, a woman in a fur scarf hurrying home as if the night were something she had failed to pay for. Zurich after midnight always has that look — polished, self-possessed, hiding its hands.

I went back to the body and opened the man’s coat. There was a photograph inside, folded twice. A woman standing by a fountain, smiling, her hand resting on a child’s shoulder. The child’s face had been scratched out with a sharp point. The woman’s had not.

I asked the officer where the body had been spotted.

“Down by the stone pier,” he said. “Current pushed it that way.”

I asked whether anyone had seen him in the water.

“Maybe a boatman. He said something was moving. He didn’t come closer.”

I looked at the man again. His eyes were half open, and the river had given him a pale, patient expression, as if he had been listening to something just before the end.

There was a name stitched into the lining of the collar.

Müller.

Just Müller. No first name, no address, no church, no city. A name a man could keep and still disappear behind.

I stood up, lit a cigarette, and watched the smoke twist into the rain. The body would be taken to the Morgue, and the watch would be inventoried, and the photograph would be put into an envelope with the rest of the dead man’s small belongings. But that night, standing there on the cold towpath, I had the feeling the Limmat had not merely released him.

It had delivered him.

And in Zurich, when the river delivers, someone upstairs knows the address.
